- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.11) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.22), model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect potential rebound.
- Model frequently overreacts to recent spikes — especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive — leading to over-forecasted peaks; apply lagged smoothing or dampen momentum.
- Mean reversion is evident in 30-day horizons: if forecast is >10% above recent 18-day average, reduce by 5–10% unless sentiment strongly supports.
- If sentiment turns negative after a spike, model often fails to correct — apply downward bias correction in next 5–7 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome is consistently below forecast (e.g., 5–10% gap), consider sentiment-driven mean reversion bias — reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period if sentiment remains weak.
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed, avoid sharp directional forecasts — use range-bound or symmetric adjustments around recent 18-day mean.
